utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment to get us ready. Yes. I'm going to start with Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, is there anything which you need to address us on immediately before the accused raises some point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have several points to raise to deal with, matters that would typically, I think, be dealt with in private session even in a fully public session. They are procedural, they deal with disclosure to the accused, matters of that sort. I'm happy to do them now or after the accused has made his point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to deal anyway with a number of administrative matters but we will start with the accused since we're in open session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, at the end of last week, when there were no hearings, I received a decision from the Registry in which I am prohibited of having any communication by telephone or any visits, and I don't understand why this came about. Are you informed of this? And I consider this to be in violent -- in gross violation of human rights, and I would request that the matter be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter we'll deal with at the moment. We will look to see what the point is, and if necessary, we'll come back to it in due course. For the moment, we will deal with those matters which are concerned with this particular issue. Yes, you want to go into private session, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in open session? Yes. There are two -- three matters, potentially, which we have to address at this stage. The first is the extent, if any, it is appropriate with this important witness to have any evidence given under Rule 89(F), he dealing with the accused very substantially on conversations, some of which have been in dispute, in some cases heavily in dispute. And it would therefore seem to us to be appropriate that those matters should be dealt with in open session. We are concerned at the evidence which it is proposed to be given about the conflict - I'm referring to the end of the statement - and the amount of resultant cross-examination which there must be, in fairness, if the evidence is given. And finally, we have to deal with the admissibility of the book as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General Clark, I'm sorry you've been brought in. There is a misunderstanding. But it doesn't matter because we're going to have a debate about the extent of your evidence and how much we're going to admit; and unless anybody objects, it seems to me, if you don't mind sitting, listening, it may be no harm is done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to the second of the points that the court expressed as being a matter of concern, could the Court possibly identify the particular passages which you say are concerning because of the degree to which they would open up cross-examination? There's 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, the question of live evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can tell you we have in mind that the witness's evidence should be given in live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It's a matter entirely for the Court. As Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you know, when we first instituted 89(F) statements, we said we would apply comprehensively in order not to take any advantage by selecting that which would be given live. We're entirely in the Court's hands. For our part, there are both exchanges where the previous witness, Klaus Naumann, was present, which might have fallen for different consideration, and there are passages where the accused is not present but other named persons are. It had occurred to us those might have been stronger candidates for 89(F) but we don't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Next, the book. We've had a chance of reading those passages on which you rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And they amount to some 10 per cent, if that, of the total pages in the book; 40-odd pages against 400-odd pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And having read the statement, it seem us to broadly that they cover the same material in the most important part, and the others, I should have thought, were not of such significance that they should be admitted. But in any event, there is the question of principle, which is how right it is for a small part of a book to allow the admission of the whole, which of course deals with much broader matters, and we are therefore minded not to admit the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are, of course, in the Court's hands, and it may be something that falls for better consideration at the end rather than at the beginning of the evidence and cross-examination. We provided you with only a limited number of pages in order, we hoped, to help and to save the Chamber from the burden of having to go through the totality of the book. We've considered the admission of the book against the rulings that have been made under Rule 70, because of course those follow on an application for limitation of evidence made by us as part of the necessary Rule 70 agreements and requirements, and there is an argument that examination, or certainly cross-examination, outside the identified pages would be in contravention of the ruling of the Chamber. We considered that yesterday with both the witness, his lawyers, but more importantly perhaps the United States government lawyers, and I think that the view taken was that a practical approach might be to say could the whole book be admitted and the witness would be happy to answer questions on anything within its ambit. But if the Court is at first sight and at this stage inclined towards the view that less rather than more is appropriate, we, I think, are happy to go along with that and await the position at the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's the course that we will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, Your Honour said that there were particular passages of the statement that might have led to broader cross-examination or more extensive cross-examination that could be allowed for in the time available for this witness. I'm not sure exactly which paragraphs the Court had in mind, because we could consider them and see to what extent we really wish them to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you may wish to consider paragraphs 39 onwards, which deal entirely with the conflict. Now, it's a matter for you what course you want to take, but the issue is if such evidence is given, what cross-examination it opens up in fairness to the trial as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may -- on the assumption that we go beyond the first break, may I come back to that immediately after the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And I suppose the final issue is timing. How long do you anticipate you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wouldn't have thought that my examination of the witness will last very much more than one session, one ordinary one-and-a-half-hour session. The statement is compact, and the witness knows his material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the witness has made himself available, as we have in our order stated, for two days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I haven't actually technically asked him when his return flight is. My oversight, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt that can be done. Mr. Kay, can you assist us whether you or Mr. Tapuskovic intend to ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter so far in relation to the book, in my view, it would be probably the position that we can take stock at the end of the evidence to see where we are. We've often made decisions at the start and ended up changing them by the finish of testimony. In terms of time for cross-examination, the amici would request half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't quite understand the position of this witness since my understanding was that he would be testifying in closed session and that you described that as a temporarily closed session, and then, in the meantime, representatives of the government of his country may be able to review the transcript, to approve some of it, to redact some of it possibly, and only then to release it to the public. I am not aware of any legal court in the world delegating its authority of this kind to any government. This would be the first time for any such thing to happen. Of course, you consider yourself to be a legal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not going to argue this point. We have made our order. The reason that the government have any rights in the matter at all is this, that in order to provide information to this Court, it is occasionally - and I stress occasionally - necessary for governments to do so, and they are allowed to do so under our Rules on certain terms, and these are one of the terms which has been followed in this case. Yes, Mr. Nice. Perhaps we should begin, and we will ask General Clark to take the declaration if he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I diffidently remind Your Honour that you were going to make some rulings. I didn't know if you intended to make them before the witness started his evidence. No. Very well. My misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think all the necessary rulings have been made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Wesley Clark; correct?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And General Clark, for you are indeed a general, your history is set out in a summary of your life which is at tab 2 of a bundle of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that bundle be given a comprehensive exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There is an issue as to whether tab 1 should be admitted because we've not admitted it under Rule 89(F). But we'll -- what we'll do is we'll give the bundle a general number and we can review the position at the end as to which tabs are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness at some stage have the bundle of exhibits -- may the witness at some stage have that bundle of exhibits if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And General Clark, without going through your personal history in detail, for it's a matter of public record, does it include that you graduated from West Point in 1966, from 1994 to 1996 you served as Director for Strategic Plans and Policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsibilities for worldwide United States military strategic planning; that from 1996 to 1997 you served as Commander-in-Chief of the United States Southern Command, Panama, where you were responsible for the direction of the United States military activities in Latin America and the Caribbean; and from 1997 through to May of 2000 you were NATO Supreme Allied Commander and Commander-in-Chief of the United States European Command, and in this position you commanded the Operation Allied Force which was NATO's first major combat action in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Clark, your first encounter with the accused, I think, was on the 17th of August of 1995 where you met him as one of a delegation that included Richard Holbrooke and the late Joseph Kruzel and others, including Colonel Drew and Robert Frasure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was this part of shuttle negotiations for a Bosnian peace deal?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us a little of the setting: What was the topics, who was running it, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Richard Holbrooke was the leader of the American delegation, and this was our first meeting with Serb President Slobodan Milosevic. We wanted to meet each of the leaders in the Balkans and present to them the general outline of what we believed to be a possible settlement that could be achieved, including a settlement achieved with the presence of some American troops as part of a NATO mission. And this was the first meeting with President Milosevic. We went to -- went to his office there in the capital of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one of the topics who should be representing the Bosnian Serbs in negotiating a peace plan; and if so, what was the accused's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. This was the question, because it had come up previously that some people were talking to Karadzic, and we wanted to raise this issue with Slobodan Milosevic, and so we asked him. "Should we be dealing with you or should we be dealing with the Bosnian Serbs?" And then President Milosevic said, "With me, of course." And as we continued the dialogue, we said, "Well, why?" And the basic reason was that he could deliver the peace agreement. And this -- this seemed improbable on the face of it; he was the president of a different country. And he said -- he said, "No. Give me the terms of the agreement, we'll have an election, a referendum on this agreement." And we said, "Well, why would a referendum in a different country bind the Bosnian Serbs?" He said, "They will not go against the will of the Serb people."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There came a time when you spoke to him with only one or perhaps a couple of people present, I think.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give the setting for that and then tell the Court your recollection of precisely what was said.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, after we had this exchange, a break was taken and Ambassador Holbrooke went up to visit the facilities outside. The meeting generally broke up. President Milosevic stayed there. And Assistant Secretary Kruzel and I approached President Milosevic as he was standing there in a casual setting outside the formal meeting, and I was still wrestling with the idea as to how it is that Milosevic could maintain that he had the authority and the power to deliver the Serb compliance with the agreement. And so I simply asked him. I said, "Mr. President, you say you have so much influence over the Bosnian Serbs, but how is it then, if you have such influence, that you allowed General Mladic to kill all those people in Srebrenica?" And Milosevic looked at me and he paused for a moment. He then said, "Well, General Clark," he said, "I warned Mladic not to do this, but he didn't listen to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your understanding of what he was referring to, if you have an understanding beyond the words themselves, can you give it to us?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And explain, if it does have a context and understanding, how you arrive at that understanding.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it was very clear what I was asking was about the massacre at Srebrenica. When I said "kill all these people," it wasn't a military operation, it was the massacre. And this was in fact what had been in the news. It had been the starting point for the international agreements which led to NATO's increased resolve to see an end to the fighting in the Balkans. So it was very clear what I was asking. It was also, to me, very clear what Milosevic was answering. He was answering that he did know this in advance, and he was walking the fine line between saying he was powerful enough, influential enough to have known it but trying to excuse from himself the responsibility for having done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next meeting, I think, was on the 13th of September, or a subsequent meeting was on the 13th of September at the accused's lodge near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 of the statement serving as a summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Milosevic on this occasion with expectations that he might be able to make some contact with Mladic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we had never -- we had never expected when we went to this meeting that there would be a meeting with Mladic and Karadzic. This was a surprise. This was during the period of the bombing. May I just ask? I have a technical problem with this computer. Maybe this button was hit or something, and I don't know which button to turn it back on with. Thank you. We went there as part of their shuttle diplomacy, and the bombing was going on. President Milosevic had been saying this bombing was bad for peace, and we of course were -- the bombing was part of the pressure to convince the Serbs to fall back and release the grip of terror on Sarajevo. And Milosevic asked the delegation, he said, "Would you be willing to meet with Karadzic and Mladic?" And Ambassador Holbrooke called us aside, he said, What do you think? These men are now indicted war criminals, should we meet with them in the interest of trying to stop and change the situation on the ground? And the delegation agreed with Holbrooke that we should do this. Holbrooke conveyed that information to Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Milosevic said, "Well, they're here. You'll see them in just a couple of minutes, they're only a couple of hundred metres away." We were surprised. We didn't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next topic: Did you form a view as to the VJ and Serb leadership receiving operational reports from the VRS? If so, what was the view and why?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It was our view that the Serb military, that the VRS was closely connected to the military of the -- of Yugoslavia, the VJ. We knew this from electronic evidence, from reliable sources, and we even at one point went and told the Serb military that they had to turn off the air defence connectivity that linked the air defence system in Bosnia with that in Serbia. So there was a clear connection. We knew that the Serb military had been -- had been carved out of the Yugoslav military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you asked Serb military to turn off the transmission, which particular Serb military leader did you address?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It was General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the Dayton negotiations, did you meet somebody called Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he introduced to you as?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He was introduced to me as the head of the Serb intelligence service. He had been -- he'd been rumoured to be very, very influential, and some people were surprised that he was at the negotiations, but there he was, and we all met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The military annex drawn at the Dayton negotiations, did you deal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with Krajisnik and ask him to review a proposed military annex? If so, what happened and how was the problem resolved?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: We did meet with the Bosnian Serb delegation. I did hand the military annex draft to Mr. Krajisnik and ask him to consider this. I told him I'd like to have an answer back in the next day or two. This was early on in the negotiations. And subsequently he did give me the paper back, and most of the annex was simply lined through. It had the effect of completely obviating the military annex. It would have put a military force into Bosnia that had no authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you attempt to resolve it? How was it resolved as a problem?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: President Milosevic had previously said that if there were any difficulties, to please consult with him. I arranged to see President Milosevic, said that the Bosnian Serbs had rejected this military annex, and asked for his help. He said, "Just give it to Milutinovic and he'll take care of it." And that's exactly what happened. A day or so later, I got it back from then-Foreign Minister Milutinovic. He said, "This is it." There were a couple of minor changes at the beginning of the document, but all those portions which had been excised by the Bosnian Serbs were restored. I thanked Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did this reveal to you about where the decision-making power lay?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it revealed to me that President Milosevic was fully in charge of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During Dayton, was time spent going over military maps of various kinds, both physical and also computer?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we did spend a great deal of time on maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one of those maps a map that you brought from America or had brought from America that's on the easel beside you?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. This is a military map that was used to discuss the boundaries around Sarajevo and whether Sarajevo would remain a divided city or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A copy of that map, Your Honours, is given the marking tab 5 of Exhibit 617.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Clark, can you, probably from where you are but with the pointer that's available, explain to the Court what the accused's part was in dealing with this map.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: This is the map that was used in the middle of the night discussion between President Milosevic and Bosnian Muslim Prime Minister Haris Silajdzic. And the discussion was, this is the city of Sarajevo, this is some of the high ground around Sarajevo, this is the discussion about which parts of the terrain would be given back to the Muslims. And as I recall the discussion, in red here -- Milosevic had this red marker and he scratched things out on it, and this was a personal -- these were personal scrawlings of the leaders here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a long time ago but, reminding yourself from the map, looking at, for example, the vertical line closer to Sarajevo that's been crossed out and the line to the east --

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I think, as I recall, this is the line that President Milosevic drew in right here and crossed this one out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And such a line would have achieved what for the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It would have given -- it would have been a give-back to the Muslims around Sarajevo. It would have been an effort to resolve this quarrel about how much ground would be given back around Sarajevo. It would have been a concession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what degree did the accused, in dealing with this map, have personal knowledge, to what degree did he appear to need to speak to or seek assistance from others with more detailed knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He appeared to have a great deal of personal knowledge and seemed to have no need to speak with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even when drawing these lines?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next, the computer map. Did you work on a computer map with the accused?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It was actually at a time prior to this, as I recall the course of the negotiations. It had to do with the corridor connecting the Bosnian Muslim held enclave of Gorazde with the bulk of the territory that was to be held by the Bosnian Muslims and by the Federation. And President Milosevic came in, we looked at the terrain from various angles, and we discussed the high ground and how much terrain would have to be surrendered to the Federation to be able to protect a road, a sovereign road out to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His level of knowledge when dealing with this issue and this computerised map?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He seemed very familiar with the road, the terrain, and the ability to draw the lines in the right place. I remember discussions about the specific area just south of Sarajevo and that road, and he was not unfamiliar with this piece of ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the end of Dayton, did the American delegation intend the Bosnian Serb leaders to initial the agreement; and if so, what was the accused's attitude as to who should be signing?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it was the intent that everyone would signal their intent, their agreement with the final document. But the Bosnian Serb delegation did not sign, and President Milosevic indicated that his initials were adequate, that he would produce the Bosnian Serb's signature later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to the computerised map, help us with this: In dealing with that map, did he turn to the Bosnian Serbs for any assistance or --

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving beyond Dayton to 1997, was there an incident involving SFOR troops who had been placed at a television antenna to guard it indeed?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a period of struggle around the city of Brcko in which NATO troops ended up on top of a piece of high ground. It so happened there was a television antenna there. We continued to occupy that antenna. One morning a mob showed up. President Milosevic had previously told me that any time there was trouble, just call him and he could handle it. I called him and I said, you're going to have to get the mob out of there, they're threatening our troops, and if you don't pull them back , we'll take other actions. He said, well, no, this is just political. I said no, it's not political, this is a threat against the troops. It seemed that within a half hour or so, the mob disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You addressed him. Was it regular for you to address him or to think of addressing him? Was there anybody to address apart from him for a problem like this?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It was clear that he still had extraordinary influence if not control. It was never clear how much, but he'd always said if there was a difficulty, call him, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 of the statement serving as a summary, and now turning to Kosovo. On the 15th of October of 1998, did you, together with Javier Solana, General Naumann fly to Belgrade to meet the accused for the purpose of getting signatures for an agreement about NATO overflight and verification?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you also going to deal with the proposed pullback of VJ and MUP forces from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You met the accused in Beli Dvor. By whom was he accompanied?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, he was accompanied by Milutinovic and Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was the upshot of that that in due course the agreement was signed? And we have that at tab --

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The air verification agreement was signed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can found that at tab 5 in the bundle -- sorry, tab 6, beg your pardon. Look at that, please. Now, when dealing with this, did the accused ask Javier Solana when the NATO ACTORD would be cancelled?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, the accused was quite anxious to have the NATO ACTORD cancelled, and he did ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Did that lead to a discussion, or indeed an argument, between him and Solana?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because Secretary-General Solana made it clear that the ACTORD couldn't be cancelled until there was compliance with the UN directives that directed the pullback of the excessive forces that had been deployed in Kosovo since February of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How consistent or otherwise was the accused's approach to Secretary-General Solana?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't consistent. I mean, at first he had denied that he'd made such an agreement, then he denied that there were any excessive forces there or any new forces that had been deployed since that period; and then, confronted with the evidence, he then relented and agreed to pull those military forces back that we had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke to him directly on the basis of information that you had, and at that time he was accompanied by General Perisic, I think.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. When he denied that there were any additional forces in there, I simply said, "Well, Mr. President, have you heard of the 211th Armoured Brigade?" We were speaking English. He said, "No, I've not heard of such a unit." He then turned and spoke to General Perisic in Serbo-Croatian, and Perisic answered him, and then Milosevic came -- turned back, looking unhappy, and said, "All right, there is such a unit." And it went this way for several different units until -- and each one he subsequently agreed to pull out. It was a grudging acceptance. It wasn't an acceptance of pulling out of the excessive units, it was an acceptance of whatever you name, we'll pull back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did General Perisic take a part in revealing the accuracy of your information for just the one example, the 211th, or was he taking a similar role in relation to other information you provided?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He confirmed the accuracy of the other two units that we provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was one of those matters you raised a police unit?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It was, but in this case this wasn't an armoured unit so General Perisic did not confirm it, and President Milosevic tried to say this wasn't a unit, it was a precinct, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did Perisic correct him on that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Perisic wasn't able to correct on that and we were left then with the issue of how many police were there and what was the -- what was the increased strength of the police. And at that point, President Milosevic promised that he would send us that information and give us a full accounting of the police elements that were in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. My oversight in relation to an earlier matter on paragraph 14. Very briefly let's cover that. In the summer of 1997, did you have conversation with Biljana Plavsic where she told you something that had been said to her by the accused about Stanisic? Just tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I did have a conversation with Biljana Plavsic, and she said that Milosevic had offered to provide security for her through Stanisic, and she rejected that offer of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And let's pick up the story at paragraph 18 of the statement serving as summary. Your next meeting on the 20th of October when you returned to Belgrade to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was raising paragraphs 27 to 28. You may want to look at those again, but you can look at them over the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at them in the sense that querying whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The mistake is mine. I was getting ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So on the 20th of October you returned to Belgrade to discuss MUP data that had been delivered by the FRY, and I think it was your intention to press further for the withdrawal of forces. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That's correct. This was a time in which we had to work an agreement to pull back the forces in compliance with the UN Security Council Resolution, and I spoke with President Milosevic. I asked that his generals cooperate in doing this. We had a full disclosure by the military and the police of what they believed to be the KLA dispositions and where their own forces were; at least, where the military forces were, the police dispositions still weren't quite complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we deal with that in just a second, but before we do, the composition of the meeting and the function of the people attending, was the accused accompanied by Milutinovic but also by a more personal advisor?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, he was accompanied by Milutinovic and, as I recall, by Goran Milinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tiny detail: The man Milinovic, what did he do in this or in any other meetings that you saw him at? What service or function did he appear to provide?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Milinovic had -- was present at almost every meeting we ever had with Milosevic. He seemed to be a Chief of Staff. He was the note-taker, he was the man who listened, who monitored, who, I guess, ensured that the directions given by Milosevic were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he did make notes?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He seemed to make notes. I recall him having a notebook and a pen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to what it's going to be Djordjevic and Perisic were able to tell you, was there at one stage a private meeting between you and the accused where you walked to an adjoining room and spoke to him about what he should do?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I began the meeting with President Milosevic on the 20th of October. There didn't seem to be a spirit of cooperation, and in front of his advisors he seemed to be wanting to again backtrack and refuse to pull the forces out and so forth. I asked him to step aside, I spoke to him one-on-one, and I warned him that if he didn't comply with the request of the United Nations, that action would be taken against him in the form of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His response?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: His response was at first to shrug this off, and then on reflection he decided that he would cooperate. He said he would ask his generals -- tell his generals to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By his response did he indicate the ability to control his generals or not?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He certainly indicated the ability to control his generals, absolutely. No question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning now then to Djordjevic and Perisic and in that order, when you spoke to Djordjevic, was there a map available?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. We laid out a map in a room off the president's office there, and General Djordjevic went through the map in some detail, pointing out the location of each of the KLA remnants that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Also present at this meeting? Do you remember who else was present?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: General Perisic was there also and he then he began to talk about the military dispositions that were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to that, can you remember who else was present? Doesn't matter if you can't at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I had with me some staff members. I had my political advisor, Mike Durkee; staff assistant Colonel Dennis Dimengo; the intelligence officer Brigadier General Glen Schaffer; and, as I recall, somewhere in this meeting also a Major General Lukic came in, another MUP officer. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your discussion with Djordjevic and in the marking of the map, was it possible to count the number of alleged KLA people concerning Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we added up these numbers and they totaled 410 KLA, according to Djordjevic's analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you raise that with him; and if so, tell us what he said.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I certainly did. I said that that you've forced -- words to the effect, you've forced 350.000, 400.000 people out of their homes; you're trying to destroy the province to get at 400 people. He said, "We were within two weeks of killing them all. Why did you stop us?" And I said, "Because you're targeting a civilian population and it's creating a humanitarian catastrophe for your own people."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you say anything further about the appropriateness of otherwise of using force?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I made it clear that that wasn't appropriate, it was illegal, against the law; it's not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's turn to Perisic who, of course, you'd recently seen being slightly counter to the accused in his force analysis or more force analysis about troop dispositions, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened with him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, he pointed out the military locations and he discussed the size of the units that were out there, and so I had a very good feel for the military dispositions and also how they were deployed tactically after I finished the discussion with General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by way of an example, how full was his information when he identified a tank?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it seemed to be very -- he was very forthcoming, I would say. Well, we saw a couple of tanks here, and he would say, yes, that's a company. Or -- I said, so if we saw a dozen vehicles here ... He'd say, yes, that's a battalion. So it indicated that we were only seeing a small portion of the total size of the force that was actually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was his approach for the army similar to or different from the approach of Djordjevic for the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He seemed to be very -- he seemed to be very forthcoming in terms of the discussion of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this meeting result in any pullback; if so, complete or partial?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: This meeting resulted in a plan for a partial pullback of some forces around Malisevo, as sort of a phase 1 of a pullback.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did this lead to another meeting four days later on the 24th, this occasion General Naumann being present?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I took this partial pullback plan. I warned them at the time that I didn't have the authority to negotiate anything for NATO. I took it back to NATO. I said NATO is going to take a look at it, at all the information you've given, and then we'll see what happens. So it turned out that General Naumann and I were sent back on the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: At this meeting we first began with President Milosevic, and there was Milutinovic there, Sainovic, Perisic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting started when and lasted how long?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It went -- the initial meeting went around 5.00, and for maybe an hour. Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your and Klaus Naumann's objective?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, the idea was to get a real pullback of all the forces and comply with the UN Security Council Resolution. We had a NATO ACTORD in place, there was a time deadline we were working against here, and we wanted to say in very direct terms to President Milosevic that this was the time that he must pull these forces back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At one stage did Perisic organise a quiet meeting with you or a private meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was that Milosevic said, well, you'll have to go back and continue to work this with these generals. So we went to Perisic first and Perisic said we're the only -- he went through the disposition, we talked about how many forces could be pulled back reasonably, and -- but he said that only President Milosevic could give the authority to pull these forces back. And he warned us, and he asked me, he said, "Please not destroy the Yugoslav military." He said, "This is the last democratic institution in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he said that, had he made arrangements about the number of people present to hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, he had. He made sure everybody else was out of the room except the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as a result of this, did you have hopes that you might accelerate the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That seemed to be a very -- a promising attitude, but on the other hand, we recognised that Milosevic had total control of what was going to be decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then make a decision as to whether you were going to achieve a full pullback or whether you needed to take things further with the accused?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: At that point it was clear that we'd gotten as far as we were going to get with Perisic, and so we decided to go back and see Milosevic and his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion -- this again back at Beli Dvor. On this occasion were others present, some you were meeting for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, Sainovic was there. As I recall, that's the first time I'd met Sainovic. The police people came in, and we assembled the whole group again. This must have been around 8.00 or 9.00 at night on that Saturday night, the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the accused's initial reaction at this part of the adjourned or however you describe it meeting?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we said to the accused essentially that we didn't get any satisfaction, or this is not enough. And I said General Naumann has an idea. General Naumann and I had talked about this previously, I turned to him and he said, you're going to have to pull these excess police back, just pull them all back, Mr. President. That's the only way to solve this problem, that's the only way to get rid of the ACTORD. All the excess police out. And Milosevic looked startled, and then he excused himself. He went back into another room with his team. They were in there for about 15 minutes, 20 minutes, and then they came back into the meeting room with us. And Milosevic agreed in principle and then he said, you'll have to continue the discussions now and work out the details of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With whom were you instructed to work out details?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: We went back at that point to the Serb Ministry of Defence, and as I recall, it was Foreign Minister Milutinovic, General Perisic, Djordjevic, Lukic, and I think Sainovic was still there. He went in and out, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did those negotiations continue until the early hours of the following morning, the 25th of October, when you returned to see the accused at Beli Dvor?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. These negotiations ended, I think, around -- between 4.30 and 5.00 on the morning of the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you saw the accused at what time, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: As I recall, it was around 9.00. We had the results at that point. We cleaned up, I checked back in with headquarters, and so we went back around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And now you were now in a position to require reduction of rather more than you'd originally identified as the number?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, the problem was -- yes, that's correct, because General Naumann had given the number of excess police at 3.000. The correct number was 4.000, so we had to go in and see Milosevic. He said he wanted to make some changes in the agreement. We said fine, we listened to him, we said now we want to make a change in the agreement; it's not 3.000 police, it's 4.000 police that have to be pulled out. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he accept that or did he resist that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: With reluctance, he accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he attempt an argument about accepting more MUP presence?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did he base that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He essentially said he wanted to stand on the original 3.000 figure. He said, Where did you get the information of 4.000? I said it came from your own documents. He had given us the documents as a result of the 15 October meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The argument to have more MUP present, was that from Milosevic or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: We were only talking -- as I recall the meeting, we were only talking to Milosevic at this point. There had been discussion the previous night with Milutinovic about the numbers of MUP and whether they could be there and be out of uniform and so forth, but on Sunday morning, Milosevic presented his changes that he wanted, we considered them, we agreed to some of them, we explained the rationale for the document, and then we presented this change and we said you're going to have to take 4.000 not 3.000 out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During this part of the negotiations, did there come a time when the accused referred to historical events going back to 1946; and if so, from recollection, can you tell the Court what it was he said and what effect it had on you?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: We achieved agreement and then it remained to type up the agreement and get it signed, and so this must have been 10.30, 11:00 in the morning or something, and President Milosevic was musing philosophically about this. And he turned to me and said, "General Clark," he said, "We know how to handle these murderers, these rapists, these criminals." He said, "We've done this before." I said, "Well, when?" He said, "In Drenica in 1946." And I said, "What did you do?" He said, "We killed them." He said, "We killed them all." I was stunned at the vehemence with which he spoke, and I just looked at him. General Naumann looked at him, as I recall, and Milosevic then said -- then he qualified his statement. He said, "Of course we did not do it all at one. It took some time."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say how long it took?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I don't recall him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The agreement being retyped, as you -- or typed, as you've explained, when it was brought in for signature, what did you notice about those who were to sign?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That Milosevic -- I noticed that Milosevic's name wasn't on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you raise that with him? What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I did raise it with him. He said it wasn't necessary. I said, well, it is necessary, and asked him to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you indeed have to press him to sign it and explain the level of people that you typically dealt with in your negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I did have to press hard on this because it's been my experience in dealing with leaders in this part world, and with President Milosevic, that they typically didn't like to sign documents because it meant then that they could no longer disavow them. And I was determined that President Milosevic would sign this. We had negotiated it with him, he had the authority. And had he not signed it, my concern was that he would have then been able to say, "Well, I didn't really see this," and he would have been able to disavow it, so his signature on that document was very important because it represented his promises to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document has already been exhibited as Exhibit 94, tab 3. Perhaps it can just be laid on the overhead projector for the witness to see the way the signature was placed. I haven't got it on the screen I think myself. I don't know if the Judges see it. Yes, there it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we can see, no place on the typed version for the accused to sign. You and General Naumann required him to sign. Just show us where, please.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Right. This is the signature block. This was typed up in Yugoslavia, in Belgrade, there while I talked to Milosevic. And these were the signatures that he wanted on there and this is what was typed on there, and of course it had our names, General Naumann's name and my name on it, and then this is where he signed it at our insistence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And this document is the record of the meeting on the 25th of October of 1998, and that is agreed being set out in an attached statement. I turn to paragraph 30, the 20th of December of 1998. Did you go to Belgrade on this occasion to meet a person new to you, Colonel General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I did. We knew that Perisic was in trouble and, based on the atmosphere in the meetings in October, I was not surprised that he was replaced by General Ojdanic, and I wanted to be certain that General Ojdanic understood the obligations that Yugoslavia had accepted through the Milosevic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who else was present on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sainovic was there. Apparently I wasn't going to be allowed to meet with General Ojdanic without Mr. Sainovic being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time, what was your judgement about this? What did it say about the level of confidence or trust reposed in Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It said that Ojdanic wasn't sufficiently trusted to meet alone with me with the interpreters present, that he needed the political guidance of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you raise -- really to raise with Ojdanic the presence of VJ tanks north of Pristina near Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. At that point, we had already seen the evidence of the violation of Milosevic's commitments to NATO. They'd already been deploying tanks north of Pristina along the main line of communication near Podujevo, and I raised this with General Ojdanic, and he said, well, it was a training mission. Well, these weren't training missions. And under the agreement, they would have had to have been notified in advance and they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In giving his answer to you, did he speak without assistance or did he discuss the matter at all first with Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Each answer that he gave me was first coached with Sainovic or cleared with Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made an assessment of Ojdanic. I don't know whether you made it there and then at this meeting or later, but what was your assessment?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I thought he was a place-holder; someone ambitious enough to want the job and maybe someone who wouldn't ask too many of the tough questions that gotten General Perisic in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Racak. Following that event, did you and General Naumann travel to Belgrade on the 19th of January to meet the accused and to attempt to arrange investigation of the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have objectives about Ambassador William Walker as well?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we wanted Ambassador Walker to remain in the country, and we only wanted Milosevic to reaffirm and maintain his commitments that he'd made to NATO in the 25 October document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting was in Beli Dvor. How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: This meeting in Beli Dvor lasted seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Milosevic was accompanied by whom on his side?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I recall Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one of the topics you raised in this long meeting the possibility of the then-ICTY Prosecutor Louise Arbour being permitted access to investigate the Racak massacre?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first topic that we raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused's reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: He employed several different lines of reaction. First he reminded us that he had never agreed to the jurisdiction of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. International Criminal Tribunal inside Yugoslavia. We then said you've promised to cooperate with the ICTY. Then he said there was no massacre, and then he said, well, there were bodies. And then we continued to persist. He said that Ms. Arbour could come as a tourist. First he said she couldn't come, then she could as a tourist but she'd have to be escorted, then she'd have to be escorted by the minister of justice. She couldn't investigate anything. Then she could look at the bodies but she could only look at them with other people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As these proposals were made, did you relay them to Justice Arbour for her reaction?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I called her several times, in each case affirming her opinion of the various offers that Mr. Milosevic made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did your exchanges with the accused on this topic end?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Essentially it came to the point that he was not offering her a satisfactory opportunity to come and do the investigation, and he continued to dance around the issues and failed to comply with what was required. So I posed it to him in very simple terms. I said, if you don't want her to come, just say so, if you don't want her to come. Otherwise, let her come, give her the authority to do the investigations properly. He said, no, he didn't want her to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to Ambassador Walker, the accused's attitude in relation to him, how was it resolved?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Milosevic continued to say that Ambassador Walker had violated his responsibilities as a diplomat by labelling this as a massacre and that it was the decision of the Serb government that he had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion, or a short exchange in any event, with Milutinovic about this during a break?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. By this time, as I recall, Milutinovic was no longer the foreign minister of Serbia but he was the president of Serbia and Milosevic had moved up to be president of Yugoslavia. But Milutinovic said, on the side, he says, "Now this is going to be -- you could get a compromise on this. This is -- listen to what -- what President Milosevic is saying, he's saying in essence it's the will of the government. So he's offering a compromise. He might not -- he might give in on this."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, there was any conclusion to this part of the --

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. There was not a conclusion other than the fact that Milosevic seemed to be determined that Walker must leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the October agreements -- commitments were concerned, what was the accused's attitude; compromising or uncompromising, what?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Milosevic told me, he said, "I'm not going to comply with these agreements. I warned you that we would 'defend ourselves,' and so we're not complying with these agreements."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your reaction to that? What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I explained to him that his actions went well beyond any reasonable defence, they were disproportionate, they violated the agreements, and I said that "If you persist in this, NATO is going to tell me to start moving aircraft." In other words, implying that he was not living up to his terms of the agreement and NATO would then invoke the ACTORD.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you in your exchanges with the accused take a strong line, make reference generally to what he was doing to his country?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I put this in terms that he could understand what the consequences would be for him and his international position. I said that, "NATO is going to be asking -- these leaders are going to be asking what is it that you are trying to do to this country? You forced professors to sign loyalty oaths, you have crushed democracy, you have taken a vibrant economy, you've wrecked it. They're going to be asking, what kind of a leader are you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did that lead the accused to say and do?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, President Milosevic became very angry and he then -- he claimed that there were no loyalty oaths, that Serbia was a democracy, and he accused General Naumann and me of threatening him. He -- he said, "You are the war criminals."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you try and calm him down?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to get back to rational discussion, and so he did calm down, but we never made any more progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at one point in this meeting did you refer back to something that you understood the accused had said to Ambassador Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Holbrooke had told me that Milosevic had said at one point that Kosovo is more important than his neck. And I asked Milosevic to confirm that, and he said, "No, that's not correct, I said it's more important than my head," meaning that that was the centre of Serbian civilisation, and that's -- that was the essence of what he was saying, that that was the key to his political future.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the earlier occasion there had been reference to what happened in 1946. Was there any further reference to that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I believe there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm three paragraphs short of the place you've asked me to start a reconsideration. We've been going just an hour. I don't know if that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the break now. General Walker --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's General Clark, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General Clark. We have to warn all witnesses, as we do, not to speak about their evidence until it's over. Could I do the same with you. We understand that you're giving a lecture tonight on international relations. Of course that's fine, but formally I must, of course, tell you not to discuss the case during it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 36 in the statement serving as summary. General Clark, when were you first aware of any FRY forces being involved in an offensive in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we started to see indicators of this and we began to hear the indicators in January. We had already seen the forces violating the agreement, we knew it was just a matter of time. As I said, in late December we saw the forces moving out, we continued to see more forces deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the Podujevo area? And what did you learn of and when there?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, these were the first ones moving out in December 1998 that I had warned General Ojdanic about on my visit down there, on about the 20th of December of 1998 and -- and then we continued to see those forces deployed out there. They manoeuvred around. And as far as we could determine, what they were doing is they would go around a village, they would stir up trouble, they would look for opportunities to use force, use their guns, heavy guns and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, and from memory if you can, of course, any elements of any particular armoured brigades that you can bring to mind as having featured at this time?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: We continued to watch the 211th Armoured Brigade because it had been pulled out. We had seen it in there earlier, it came back in to the border and then began to deploy inside Kosovo again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the Pristina Corps did you notice anything or were you informed of anything as to its level of arms?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we saw it being reinforced. It was the command and control headquarters for the province and we saw reinforcements added to it so that it became much more capable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a judgement as to the degree to which it had been enlarged?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It may have been doubled in strength. It had a lot of additional forces with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get to learn of something called a Joint Command? And if the answer is yes, can you indicate your source of knowledge in the most general terms, and what you understood that to be.

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I had two general sources of knowledge. First I had received some kind of an indication when I'd first met Sainovic, and the accused had introduced him as being someone who was in charge of this. And then it was clear from other reliable sources that there had actually been a joint -- some kind of a joint police and army headquarters established to be able to deal with the region and that Sainovic had some kind of a role in that. Perhaps a role that enabled him to undercut the authority of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What purpose could you see in the use of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, first it was necessary to -- it would have been necessary to coordinate the military and police activities on the ground, but it served an adjunct purpose as well because it avoided the direct control of the armed forces by the General Staff, and just following on from the comments that Perisic had made to me, I assumed that there were still elements within the General Staff which might have not been under the full political control of President -- then President Milosevic, then thus enabling him to bypass whatever resistance there might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In early March of 1999, did Secretary-General Solana give you some instructions as to what you were to do so far as General Ojdanic was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. We continued to see the build-up of these forces and I brought them to Solana's attention. He said okay, you got to call and ask him -- tell Ojdanic to stop bringing those troops in. See if you can give him a warning to stop doing it so it doesn't escalate the crisis further. And I did call Ojdanic, and I told him we were watching what he was doing, I asked him not to do this. He replied that -- that we were causing him to do this, that he was doing this in self-defence against the threat of a NATO invasion. And of course there was -- there was no possibility of NATO invasion at that point. I told Ojdanic that he shouldn't do it. He said that there were forces coming in to Macedonia. I explained that these forces weren't sufficient for an invasion and warned him that he was violating the October 1998 agreement, that I had met with him on the previous December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With what military or other objective was the build-up of troops consistent in your then-judgement, General?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: All of this was consistent with the plan that we'd heard rumoured to seek the final solution to this problem in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seek the final solution by what --

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: That is to say by using a large-scale ethnic cleansing operation against the people in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the Chamber's observations about paragraphs 39 to 45, with your leave I will deal with the first sentence of paragraph 39 and with paragraph 41, subject to laying a foundation for knowledge, and not the balance. I don't know if that will be acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is simply a question of the extent of cross-examination which is to be let in by it, but that's the only point that we make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that and we're grateful for the concern that the Chamber has expressed through that question to me. The first sentence of paragraph 39 is a simple point. Paragraph 41 is a matter of pattern evidence, pattern connecting between one conflict and another, and I will be seeking first the witness's account of his knowledge for that sort of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, on what day or approximately what day, in your judgement, did the Serb offensive begin?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Either Friday the 19th or Saturday the 20th, as NATO could best determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your statement you deal with -- it happens at paragraph 41 but don't refer to that, please. You deal with the pattern of events, a typical pattern of events where the VJ and other units came to be involved. Before I ask you for what that pattern was, can you explain what your sources of information were in the most general terms so that we can understand how you could form this judgement?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: I got this from both the news media and other reliable sources. So it was a combination of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the pattern of involvement of the VJ, the MUP, and/or other units?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It seemed consistent with an earlier pattern that we had observed over the decade of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Namely that the military surrounds an objective, it blocks it, it prevents reinforcement or exit. The police then go through, they arrest people by name if they have particular information, that they search for. The paramilitaries then go in and threaten people and rob them and so forth, and then people are thrown out of their homes afterwards, all under the control of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The pattern that you've identified, was it something in your judgement as a soldier that could have happened with or without the knowledge of the local VJ or the local MUP?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Could not have happened without the coordination of the VJ and the MUP, and based on what I'd seen of the army, it had to have happened with high-level command and control because this was still a disciplined force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to return to one topic you dealt with earlier and ask you a couple of further questions about it. It's the air defence system. You will remember telling the Chamber, that's paragraph 6, how you once told Perisic to turn off the transmission system. Can you amplify what you've already said about the air defence system, describing in a sentence what your judgement was of its nature, contrasting it with or comparing it with air defence system cooperation of, say NATO countries or the United Kingdom and the United States, something like that?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, this was an integrated air defence system that was put together coherently, laid out on a single template with various regional reporting nodes and a dispersed early warning radars and target acquisition radars and a certain number of missile launching sites and so forth. And it was a leftover from Yugoslavia, and it was still fully operational so it indicated to me that this was as though there had never been a separation between the VRS and the VJ; it was simply an integrated air defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How would that compare with, say, information sharing between allies such as the United Kingdom and the United States, something like that, in general terms without saying anything that would be revealing about particular relationships current at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, under NATO agreements, countries delegated their air defence to NATO but it was still under a sovereign agreement. So there was data sharing between nations but it was data sharing over national systems. So there was an international system on top. So what you've got right here is what was formerly a national system that had never been disestablished, it was still there in the case of Yugoslavia. Integrated. That means all the pieces would fit together. Information would flow back and forth. As far as we could tell, it was seamless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the significance of this, what does it -- and what does it reveal about the relationship between the two armies concerned?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: Well, as we looked at this, our reliable information seemed to suggest that the separation of the two armies was -- it was political but it wasn't substantive. In other words, that what had happened is that when these two armies separated, as best we could figure this out, soldiers who had lived in the republic -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina were taken out of the VJ, but the officers were shuffled in a general sense. Some officers volunteered to serve there apparently, others didn't. The training was still done, as far as we could determine, inside and by the VJ. Officer assignments were controlled by the VJ, and promotions and pay were subject to the control of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm more concerned about being specific to the air defence system, its integrated nature. What does that reveal about the connection of the two armies?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: It meant that there was an integrated control of the system so that decisions to fire or decisions to turn on radars and so forth were likely to have been made by Yugoslavia, not by the Serbs themselves in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just now deal with the present position so far as exhibits are concerned. If the summary of General Clark's background may become tab 2. For the time being we pass over tab 3, but I'd just ask the witness this as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You wrote the book "Waging Modern War." Have you become aware since writing it of any corrections communicated either to you or to your publishers?

utterances.speaker: WESLEY CLARK
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a chart that shows passages that the Prosecution have asked the Judges to have in mind from that book, and indeed at tab 4 -- at tab 3, you have, I think, the excerpts from the book, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the question is this: We're not going to admit that. Do you want -- sorry I don't understand the position. Are you saying that the book -- that the accused is free to cross-examine on any part of the book? That is not as I had understood the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not what we're seeking, especially in light of what Your Honour was saying this morning. So that even the extracts, it may be, don't need to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, most certainly not because it seems to me there is an unfairness in producing extracts which in any event are being given in evidence largely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. At tab 5 I said there was an interest in the exhibit from a museum. There is letter which doesn't need to become an exhibit but can be distributed. Alternatively, it could become part of tab 5, the map. It comes from the MacArthur Museum of Arkansas Military History, and it explains the only change made to the map is the addition of a pencil accession number, which it identifies. So it may be that this letter could become part of tab 5, particularly if the Chamber is prepared to accept the copy version of the map as tab 5 in order to allow the original to return to the museum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that now

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will accept the versions that we have; the original can return to the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there are two maps in tab 5, one of which isn't dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
